notes: Three site-level native signed-lag correlations already exist, but all span both sides of exact matching. Raw annual rows can support one-sided re-extraction where sample size permits.
Nopporo 1999-2017 extends IWE001; useful for directional geometry but not an independent programme.
Bee abundance rises through season while visitation to focal flowers declines; calendar date cannot be treated as one partner-relative window.

Final intact fruit set is available across flowering timing, but the focal Phaulernis window is inferred from oviposition/egg observations and therefore describes realized interaction timing, not independent adult availability.
Strong antagonist-mediated flowering-time selection across 20 populations and two years; partner-relative activity remains unresolved.
Early/late flowering links seed predation and offspring fitness, but the predator window is imported from earlier literature rather than measured contemporaneously.
Early versus late flowering separates pollination and seed-predation consequences in a Hadena system; full extraction must preserve benefit, cost and net channels separately.
Hadena-dominant versus co-pollinator-dominant windows are measured directly and successful fruits are post-predation; quantitative use awaits raw variance verification.
Experimental flowering cohorts are independently ordered by same-season pollinator visitation; final mature seed set is extracted.
2007 early versus middle flowering is ordered by contemporaneous bumble-bee activity and linked to final natural seed set.
Flowering rank and attack demonstrate temporal escape, but realized seed set is model-derived without recoverable variance and cannot serve as final fitness.
Peak and late windows are ordered by measured Centris activity and linked to natural-pollination seed set.
Herbivory timing is experimentally manipulated and viable seed production is measured. This identifies sensitivity to interaction timing but not a natural partner-availability window.

Female butterfly flight is independently measured and plant ramets are followed to dehiscence. The preflight already preserves core-vs-early and core-vs-late separately; numeric 2012-2014 female timing remains the blocker.

Source-reported total-egg and active-egg Gaussian curves show host-stage filtering shifts the effective antagonist peak +0.49 flowering-date SD and narrows sigma from 0.92 to 0.66. This is realized/effective cost geometry, not independent adult-flight timing.

Independent Portuguese Gentiana-Phengaris programme: 127 shoots and 837 eggs show offspring survival varies with host bud size/developmental stage and oviposition period. Replicates host-stage filtering of raw exposure, but does not measure final plant fitness.

Yucca glauca resource allocation makes late distal flowers more likely to abort when basal fruits are present; all Tegeticula eggs in aborted flowers die. Taxonomically distinct host filter; mechanism only, no final plant-fitness effect.

Source Equation 1 propagates the active-egg Gaussian through observed intact-RU fractions and larval survival to final fitness. High-fecundity trough predicts 29.98% loss from baseline; medium predicts 13.72%. Same Cardamine dependence cluster; not independent adult-flight evidence.

Geum urbanum × Byturus ochraceus: predation occurred almost exclusively in the first flowering peak; among predated plants final total seed mass was maximized at an intermediate 36% of flowers in the second peak. This is a realized predator-window/final-fitness tradeoff, not independently censused adult availability.

Ulex europaeus common garden: long-flowering plants escape the seed-predation peak in time, while short-flowering plants fruit during the peak but reduce attack partly via predator satiation. Whole-season infestation is nearly identical (29% vs 30%), and maternal flowering type has no significant effect on annual pod or seed production; retained as a null/boundary against a timing-only escape rule.

Ficus racemosa seasonal study: within-tree reproductive asynchrony is similar across seasons but its effect on pollinator reproduction switches from positive in winter to negative in summer. A 3-5 C warmer summer reduces fig-wasp reproduction and increases seed production nearly two-fold, largely through smaller syconia/nursery size. Retained as a mixed boundary showing climate/nursery-size modulation rather than partner-window timing support.

Yucca filamentosa × Tegeticula cassandra: peak flowering date negatively predicts pollinator/day in both 2001 (-0.37) and 2002 (-0.27), while pollinator/day positively predicts relative fruit set (+0.60,+0.48). Strong independent service-window mechanism but fruit set is pre-larval-cost, so not mixed net fitness.

Senita cactus × Upiga virescens: exclusion experiments show co-pollinator buffering is conditional on temporal access. Hot late seasons close flowers before sunrise and exclude diurnal bees; in July 1998 a gap between senita-moth cohorts coincided with 0% open-pollinated fruit set while pollen supplementation yielded 22.5±6.6%. Fruit initiation is pre-larval cost, so mechanism only.

Kula 2012 Chapter 3: individual flowering × oviposition synchrony predicts predation in opposite directions across 2008 and 2009 (chi-square 46.47 positive vs 16.74 negative, both p<0.0001). Flower/egg-to-first-larva lags were 10/5 d in 2008 versus 17/15 d in 2009, with faster fruit maturation in 2009, showing developmental phase lag can reverse effective cost geometry. Same MLBS dependence as IWE015.

Pellmyr 1989 + Després & Jaeger 1999: Chiastocheta species oviposit from flower day 1 through day 7/after flowering. Marginal pollination benefit declines with flower age as fewer ovules remain unfertilized, while larval seed cost persists; benefit-cost equality occurs around 4-5 eggs/flower and natural means span 2.3-7.25. Independent mixed-system support for stage-specific adult service versus delayed offspring cost.

Glochidion lanceolarium × Epicephala lanceolaria: adult pollination/oviposition occurs Apr-May, fruits and eggs are dormant May-Dec, eggs hatch as fruits reactivate in Jan-Feb, larvae then consume developing seeds, and adults eclose Mar-Apr. Roughly eight-month adult-service to offspring-cost lag with mature seed fate measured across four populations; no phase-lag treatment, so stage-structure evidence only.

Lathyrus vernus × Bruchus atomarius: late/distal fruits are more likely to abort, but beetles preferentially oviposit on fruits with lower future abortion probability using phenology/position plus another cue. Observed selective oviposition produces more developed beetles than random allocation (2.84 vs 2.02) and lowers plant intact-seed output relative to the random scenario. Final-fitness host-filter evidence, but timing is not isolated.

Anthocharis cardamines × five Brassicaceae hosts: host phenological state at oviposition and temperature strongly alter larval performance/developmental-race outcomes, but the probability that the initial plant outgrows the larva and forms mature seedpods depends only on host species identity. Direct boundary against assuming stage alignment automatically predicts final plant reproduction.

Rheum nobile × Bradysia: oviposited flowers have greatly reduced fruit abortion (F=287.24,p<0.001) and elevated IAA before larvae hatch (oviposition F=355.97; oviposition×day F=140.82; both p<0.001). Flowering sequence does not explain fruit set, abortion or oviposition. Mixed-system evidence that partner action can modify the host filter mapping exposure to future cost.

Dianthus sylvestris × Hadena compta: individual flowering onset is linked to fruit set, secondary predation and final relative reproductive success (% flowers producing unattacked fruits with mature dispersal-ready seeds). Final success declines through season in both 2001 (-0.037±0.009 SE) and 2003 (-0.076±0.030), while benefit/cost channel geometry differs by year. No independent adult Hadena curve, so realized-window evidence only.

Parkinsonia aculeata × Penthobruchus germaini: repeated seed-phenology and oviposition surveys show egg density drops as pods mature and fails to peak when seed availability is highest. Mean seed predation remains 2-30% despite 0.55-3.2 eggs/seed; even removing direct immature mortality, the model predicts only 5-56% predation at observed egg densities. Independent final-seed-loss evidence for temporal tracking inertia.

Early ecotype flowering-to-oviposition interval is 11.50±1.44 d versus 5.72±0.53 d late; among final-instar attacked plants, 34% versus 4% dehisce before larval completion, while 41% versus 58% are wholly consumed. Fate distributions differ chi-square(df=2)=11.95,p=0.003. Positive final-outcome phase evidence; same dependence as IWE032 and still lacks paired numeric adult-flight coordinate.

Yucca kanabensis × non-pollinating yucca moth: flowering date/fruit age strongly predict oviposition exposure, but flowering date/isolation/fruit number do not predict realized cheater larval number (n=359; model R2=0.000). Host fruit age and competition with pollinator larvae affect cheater survival, showing downstream filtering can erase an upstream phenology signal. Final seed timing effect is not inferred.\n
